issues.title: Strict CDF convention mismatches atomic Stieltjes terms
issues.failure_explanation: Let the cut be deterministically a with 0<a<1/2 and evaluate the theorem at t=a. From the definition of ell, P[ell<a]=0, whereas the displayed first Stieltjes integral includes the atom at c=a and equals a. Thus the displayed formula computes the weak CDF P[ell≤t], not the strict event asserted in the proof. The same global strict convention also conflicts with the claimed right continuity and causes analogous boundary mismatches in later atomic-distribution formulas.
issues.overall_effect: The general formulas are not literally valid for discrete or mixed cuts under the stated strict convention, despite the paper's intended inclusion of such distributions. Continuous-density cases are unaffected by boundary atoms.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Adopt the standard right-continuous CDF convention F_X(t)=P[X≤t] throughout, and change the corresponding strict event boundaries in thm - pdf and the listed dependent formulas and proofs to weak boundaries. Keep the displayed Stieltjes integrals, moment identities, independence conclusions, and convergence deductions unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The old source itself calls the CDF right-continuous, states F(0)=P[X=0], depicts the weak event in fig:region2, and uses Stieltjes integrals that include boundary atoms. These features uniquely force the weak-CDF reading, so the strict symbols are a repeated transcriptional convention error requiring no repair of the mathematical argument.

issues.title: N-fold interval-length factorization from only pairwise independence

failure_location.quote: Since the $\ell_i$ ($i>0$) are all independent, it follows that

issues.failure_explanation: The cited theorem formally states only that each pair ell_i, ell_j is independent. Pairwise independence does not justify factorizing the expectation of an n-fold product. Moreover, the old induction assumes only separate independence of r_n from each preceding factor and then treats this as independence from the whole tuple, which is not a valid implication. Thus the corollary's product factorization is not established by the available input.
issues.overall_effect: The formula E[L_n]=E[ell_1]^n is true only after mutual independence of all interval factors is established; v1 supplied only pairwise independence and an insufficient induction argument.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen thm - ind from pairwise to mutual independence and repair the induction using the invariant that (ℓ_1,…,ℓ_n,r_n) has product law. Given an independent new cut c_n, the pair (ℓ_{n+1},r_{n+1}) is a measurable function of (c_n,r_n), is independent of the preceding factors, and has the product law already established by the one-step calculation. The product expectation then follows.
issues.why_classification: Pairwise independence does not justify the displayed n-fold factorization, so this is not a typo. Nevertheless, the old one-step joint-distribution computation supplies all needed input, and a short standard strengthening of the induction proves mutual independence without new assumptions, new architecture, or any loss of the expected-length formula.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Assume that $r_n$ is jointly independent from $(\ell_i)_{i=1}^n$.

issues.title: Unsupported general exponential convergence rate

failure_location.quote: As a corollary of \Cref{thm - conv}, we may thus show that under some mild hypothesis, the distributions of the normalized roots $r_n$ always converges uniformly to the uniform distribution, and that the convergence is at least linear with the rate $1-2(\mu-\mu^{2}-\sigma^{2}) \in \bigl[\frac{1}{2},1\bigr)$ (see \Cref{fig:convergence}).

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that convergence to the uniform root law is at least linear with rate q = 1-2(μ-μ²-σ²), and the later remark propagates that rate to the law, mean, and variance of the scaling factors. The old formal support only gives, for each fixed epsilon and a corresponding delta, an estimate of the form epsilon+C(epsilon)q^k. The nondecaying error floor and potentially unbounded epsilon-dependent coefficient do not imply an O(q^k) bound; a genuine rate requires additional regularity.
issues.overall_effect: Uniform convergence was presented as having a general geometric rate, and that unsupported rate was propagated to the scaling-factor distribution and moments. The qualitative convergence conclusion is distinct from this rate overclaim.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace every unconditional assertion of a q-geometric rate, including its propagation to scaling-factor distributions and moments, by the valid statement that for each fixed ε and corresponding δ the error is bounded by ε+C(ε)q^n, which yields qualitative convergence but not a general O(q^n) rate. State a genuine q-rate only under separately specified and proved regularity assumptions.
issues.why_classification: Serious: the recorded complete correction withdraws the general geometric convergence rate and its propagation to the scaling-factor distribution and moments. The surviving fixed-tolerance estimate and qualitative convergence do not provide a comparable general quantitative rate. Removing this substantive rate guarantee is major mathematical loss even though the correction is local and qualitative convergence survives. A geometric rate under additional regularity is only a conditional repair obligation in this record, not an established complete route preserving the advertised general rate.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: The bound $\varepsilon+O(\mu_\ell^n)$ should not be interpreted as a genuine $\mu_\ell$-exponential convergence rate, since the implicit constant depend on $\varepsilon>0$ and may blow up as $\varepsilon\to0$.

issues.title: Invalid positive-operator invocation in the root convergence proof

failure_location.quote: which implies that $\mathcal{T}$ is continuous at $t=0$ and $t=1$, and thus a positive linear operator from $B_\circ[0,1]$ to $B_\circ[0,1]$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $\mathcal{T}: X \to Y$ be a positive linear operator preserving linear functions.

issues.failure_explanation: Let the cut be deterministically 1/2 and choose the nonnegative continuous function G(t)=max{1-4|t-1/2|,0}. It belongs to B_circ[0,1] and satisfies G(1/4)=G(3/4)=0 and G(1/2)=1. The displayed operator therefore gives (TG)(1/2)=0+0-1=-1. Hence T is not positive on B_circ, even though its integrand is nonnegative for the special nondecreasing functions that are CDFs. The positive-operator theorem's stated hypothesis is consequently unmet.
issues.overall_effect: The cited positive-operator theorem cannot establish the old root-law convergence theorem, even apart from the theorem's independently overbroad prior class; its downstream general convergence results consequently lack this proof input.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Discard the positive-operator invocation and replace the convergence proof by a valid argument for the actual evolution operator. The concretely established route is to derive the density transfer operator for absolutely continuous root laws, prove its L1 contraction and convergence using its polynomial eigenstructure and density approximation, and then carry that convergence through thm - pdf_general and cor - mean_variance_gen under the same hypotheses.
issues.why_classification: The counterexample proves that the operator is genuinely nonpositive on B_circ[0,1], so no local sign, estimate, or domain-description edit validates the cited theorem. The established replacement changes the state space, operator, convergence norm, and core proof mechanism for the whole affected chain; that is essentially new proof architecture, independently of the separate scope defect.

issues.title: No-endpoint-atoms condition does not ensure root-law convergence

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In order to state our results in a way that applies to all random variables on $[0,1]$, including those that do not admit a probability density function, we use the Lebesgue--Stieltjes integral.

issues.failure_explanation: Take every cut equal to 1/2 and let r₀ equal 1/3 with probability p and 2/3 with probability 1-p. These choices satisfy the old hypotheses. The stated map sends 1/3 to 2/3 and 2/3 to 1/3, so for p≠1/2 the law alternates and for p=1/2 it is stationary but nonuniform. Thus excluding endpoint atoms does not support the theorem's universal uniform-convergence conclusion. The same obstruction also occurs for atomless singular priors, as the revision demonstrates.
issues.overall_effect: The arbitrary-prior convergence theorem fails for internal atomic and singular continuous priors, and the later general scaling-factor convergence results lose their stated support in that regime.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the arbitrary-prior theorem by the established absolutely continuous version: assume r_0 has a density and P[0<c<1]>0, prove that the root densities converge to the uniform density in L1, and restrict thm - pdf_general, cor - mean_variance_gen, and all accompanying arbitrary-prior claims to that same regime.
issues.why_classification: Internal atomic and atomless singular priors are natural classes satisfying the old hypotheses yet can remain periodic or nonuniform and stationary. Restricting to absolutely continuous priors excludes the expressly advertised discrete, mixed, and singular regimes—including natural deterministic priors—and the concrete surviving theorem also requires a rebuilt convergence proof. Thus every established resolution incurs global reconstruction or major model-class loss.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Let $F$ be the cumulative distribution functions of the cuts $c_n$ and $g_n$ the probability density functions of the absolutely continuous normalized roots $r_n$.

issues.title: Missing factor two in the concluding contraction factor

failure_location.quote: On average, the convergence is linear, and the expected interval length behaves as $C^n L_0$, where $C=1-\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ is the expected contraction factor.

issues.failure_explanation: The conclusion claims that the expected contraction factor is C=1-E[c(1-c)]. The old formal calculation establishes μ_ell=1-2(μ-μ²-σ²)=1-2E[c(1-c)], and the interval-length formula uses this mean as its exponential factor. Thus the prose differs from the paper's own result by a factor of 2; for c=1/2 it gives 3/4 instead of the actual factor 1/2.
issues.overall_effect: Only the final summary formula is wrong; the earlier formal contraction and expected-length formulas already contain the correct value.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the concluding factor by C=1−2E[c(1−c)] and leave the earlier formal contraction and expected-length results unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The missing factor changes a coherent advertised exponential rate, so it should not be classified as a mere typo. However, cor - mean_variance_special and the expected-length calculation already prove the corrected value; one local summary correction resolves the issue with no additional argument, dependent repair, or mathematical loss.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: On average, the convergence is linear, and the expected interval length behaves as $C^n L_0$, where $C=1-2\,\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ is the expected contraction factor.
